chunks: "The big advantages are that you can deliver much more current, the output ripple is lower and at a higher frequency so you need less capacitance, the transient response is faster because the effective inductance is L over N, and the heat is spread over several smaller stages instead of one hot spot.
You can also shed phases at light load to keep efficiency up, and the input capacitor sees a smaller RMS ripple because the input current pulses are interleaved.
The disadvantages are cost and complexity.
You need N inductors and N pairs of FETs or power stages, a multiphase controller, per-phase current sensing and balancing, and a careful symmetrical layout.
Fixed losses like gate drive and core loss scale with the number of phases, so at light load a many-phase converter is worse unless it sheds phases.
And imbalance is a real risk: if one phase carries more current it heats first.
One subtlety I like to mention: if you compare against a single phase using the same total silicon, the conduction loss is basically the same.
The efficiency win comes from being able to use smaller, faster parts per phase, lower AC losses and phase shedding, not from the I-squared-R magically going down.
So for a 5 amps rail I stay with one phase. For a 1 volts, 60 amps processor rail with fast steps I go multiphase."
